drug_class: Biologic DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug) / Selective T-cell costimulation blocker
purpose: Abatacept is used to treat moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and certain types of juvenile arthritis. It helps reduce joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, and can slow down joint damage over time. It is often used when other arthritis medicines have not worked well enough.
how_it_works: Your immune system normally fights germs, but in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, it mistakenly attacks your own joints, causing inflammation and damage. Abatacept works by blocking a signal that activates certain immune cells called T-cells, which are responsible for that attack. By calming down these overactive immune cells, it helps reduce inflammation and protect your joints.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include headache, nausea, upper respiratory infections like the common cold, sore throat, and mild injection site reactions if you use the self-injection form. Some people may feel tired or have mild stomach upset.
warnings: Because abatacept lowers your immune system activity, you are more likely to get infections, including serious ones like pneumonia or tuberculosis. Tell your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, or signs of infection. You should not receive live vaccines while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor about any history of recurring infections, COPD, hepatitis B, or cancer before starting this medication.
typical_dosing: Abatacept can be given as an intravenous (IV) infusion at a clinic, usually once a month after the first few doses, or as a weekly injection you give yourself at home under the skin. Your doctor will decide which form and dose is right for you based on your weight and condition.
